# Step 0 — Load data

```{r load-data}
counts <- as.matrix(read.delim("data/GSE125583_raw_counts.tsv.gz",
                               row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE))
traits <- read.csv("data/GSE125583_traits.csv")
stopifnot(identical(colnames(counts), traits$sample))   # same sample order
dim(counts)
```

# Solved example — XIST and sex

Same pattern as module ↔ trait, but on one gene with a known answer.

```{r solved-example}
# 1. One value per sample: XIST (Entrez 7503) as log2 counts-per-million.
lib_size <- colSums(counts)
xist_log_cpm <- log2(counts["7503", ] / lib_size * 1e6 + 1)

# 2. Compare with the trait (drop the sample with missing sex).
xist_df <- data.frame(xist = xist_log_cpm, sex = traits$sex) |> filter(!is.na(sex))
t.test(xist ~ sex, data = xist_df)

# 3. Plot.
ggplot(xist_df, aes(sex, xist, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(F = "#E69F00", M = "#56B4E9")) +
  labs(x = "Sex", y = "XIST, log2(CPM + 1)",
       title = "XIST is expressed in females only: sex labels match the data") +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "none")

# 4. Conclusion in one sentence: XIST is far higher in females, so the sex labels are correct.
```
